# Simulation Modelling of Crop Diseases Using a Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Removed (SEIR) Model

A fork of
[{cropsim}](https://github.com/r-forge/cropsim/tree/master/pkg/cropsim)
(Hijmans *et al.* 2009) designed to make using the EPIRICE model (Savary
*et al.* 2012) for rice diseases easier to use and to implement the
EPIWHEAT model in the same R package. This version provides easy to use
functions to fetch weather data from NASA POWER, via the
[{nasapower}](https://cran.r-project.org/package=nasapower) package
(Sparks 2018) and predict disease intensity of five rice diseases using
a generic Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Removed (SEIR) model (Zadoks
1971) function,
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md).
The legacy `SEIR()` in {cropsim} uses a non-canonical formula for
“diseased” ([it accumulates “infectious” twice via
`sum(infectious)`](https://github.com/r-forge/cropsim/blob/7b7a035a612f9386112d8d49ec21724500d7f88e/pkg/cropsim/R/SEIR.R#L118C1-L120C60)).
The modern core of
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
in {epicrop} was changed to the canonical formula
(`diseased = latent + infectious + removed`), which reduced modern
diseased and COFR relative to legacy. So, please be aware that the
legacy `SEIR()` and the modern
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
will give different results for the same parameters, and that the modern
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
is more consistent with the canonical SEIR model. This modern core of
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
is also now 1 indexed, which is more consistent with R’s indexing and
makes it easier to understand the model’s parameters and outputs when
developing new models based on this core. The original `SEIR()` is 0
indexed, which is as it was used in the original EPIRICE model and
published in Savary *et al.* (2012) and the legacy `SEIR()` in
{cropsim}.

This package implements the original EPIRICE model as detailed in Savary
*et al.* (2012), which introduces the model and uses it to model global
epidemics of rice diseases illustrating the risk of bacterial blight,
brown spot, leaf blast, sheath blight and rice tungro disease.
Additional models included for rice are adapted from Kim *et al.* (2015)
for rice sheath blight and leaf blast.

The original EPIWHEAT model as presented in Savary *et al.* (2015) is
also included in this implementation and can be used to model potential
epidemics of two wheat diseases, leaf rust and Septoria tritici blotch,
is also included in this package.

Users may also provide their own parameters to the generic
[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
function to simulate other crop diseases as long as the weather data
provided meet the model’s requirements.

# Quick start

{epicrop} is not yet on CRAN. You can install it this way.

\
[`install.packages`](https://rdrr.io/r/utils/install.packages.html)`(``"epicrop"``,`\
`  repos ``=`` `[`c`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/c.html)`(``"https://adamhsparks.r-universe.dev"``,`\
`            ``"https://cloud.r-project.org"``)``)`

## Get weather data

First you need to provide weather data for the model; {epicrop} provides
the
[`get_wth()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/get_wth.md)
function to do this. Using it you can fetch weather data for any place
in the world from 1983 to near present by providing the and latitude and
dates or length of rice growing season as shown below.

\
[`library`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/library.html)`(`[`epicrop`](https://codeberg.org/adamhsparks/epicrop)`)`\
\
`# Fetch weather for year 2000 wet season for a 120 day rice variety at the IRRI`\
`# Zeigler Experiment Station`\
`wth`` ``<-`` `[`get_wth`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/get_wth.md)`(`\
`  lonlat ``=`` `[`c`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/c.html)`(``121.25562``, ``14.6774``)``,`\
`  dates ``=`` ``"2000-07-01"``,`\
`  duration ``=`` ``120`\
`)`\
\
`wth`\
`#> Key: <YYYYMMDD>`\
`#>        YYYYMMDD   DOY  TEMP  TMIN  TMAX  RHUM  RAIN     LAT      LON`\
`#>          <IDat> <int> <num> <num> <num> <num> <num>   <num>    <num>`\
`#>   1: 2000-07-01   183 25.29 23.86 27.78 92.20 23.12 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   2: 2000-07-02   184 26.13 23.54 29.90 86.01 17.34 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   3: 2000-07-03   185 25.50 24.28 27.23 94.16 29.08 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   4: 2000-07-04   186 25.81 24.50 27.56 92.42 13.01 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   5: 2000-07-05   187 25.97 25.13 27.40 92.34 32.20 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>  ---                                                                `\
`#> 117: 2000-10-25   299 25.82 23.44 29.54 89.76 12.04 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 118: 2000-10-26   300 25.44 24.14 26.99 94.93 13.03 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 119: 2000-10-27   301 25.74 24.54 27.69 91.43 11.54 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 120: 2000-10-28   302 25.44 24.72 26.62 91.90 74.20 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 121: 2000-10-29   303 24.97 24.15 26.34 94.15 29.11 14.6774 121.2556`

## Modelling bacterial blight disease intensity

Once you have the weather data, run the model for any of the five rice
diseases by providing the emergence or crop establishment date for
transplanted rice.

\
`bb_sim`` ``<-`` `[`bacterial_blight`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)`(``wth``, emergence ``=`` ``"2000-07-01"``)`\
\
`bb_sim`\
`#>      simday      dates    sites latent infectious  removed    senesced rateinf  rlex rtransfer`\
`#>       <int>     <IDat>    <num>  <num>      <num>    <num>       <num>   <num> <num>     <num>`\
`#>   1:      1 2000-07-01 100.0000      0     0.0000    0.000    1.000000       0     0         0`\
`#>   2:      2 2000-07-02 108.6875      0     0.0000    0.000    2.086875       0     0         0`\
`#>   3:      3 2000-07-03 118.1002      0     0.0000    0.000    3.267877       0     0         0`\
`#>   4:      4 2000-07-04 128.2934      0     0.0000    0.000    4.550811       0     0         0`\
`#>   5:      5 2000-07-05 139.3254      0     0.0000    0.000    5.944065       0     0         0`\
`#>  ---                                                                                          `\
`#> 116:    116 2000-10-24   0.0000      0   396.0528 1404.565 2665.037553       0     0         0`\
`#> 117:    117 2000-10-25   0.0000      0   356.3610 1444.257 2712.120592       0     0         0`\
`#> 118:    118 2000-10-26   0.0000      0   309.2779 1491.340 2755.012575       0     0         0`\
`#> 119:    119 2000-10-27   0.0000      0   266.3860 1534.232 2791.854071       0     0         0`\
`#> 120:    120 2000-10-28   0.0000      0   229.5445 1571.073 2824.358958       0     0         0`\
`#>      rremoved  rgrowth rsenesced diseased intensity     lat      lon`\
`#>         <num>    <num>     <num>    <num>     <num>   <num>    <num>`\
`#>   1:  0.00000  9.68750  1.000000    0.000         0 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   2:  0.00000 10.49959  1.086875    0.000         0 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   3:  0.00000 11.37416  1.181002    0.000         0 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   4:  0.00000 12.31499  1.282934    0.000         0 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>   5:  0.00000 13.32593  1.393254    0.000         0 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#>  ---                                                                `\
`#> 116: 43.67864  0.00000 39.691810 1800.618         1 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 117: 39.69181  0.00000 47.083039 1800.618         1 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 118: 47.08304  0.00000 42.891982 1800.618         1 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 119: 42.89198  0.00000 36.841497 1800.618         1 14.6774 121.2556`\
`#> 120: 36.84150  0.00000 32.504887 1800.618         1 14.6774 121.2556`

Lastly, you can visualise the result of the model run.

\
[`library`](https://rdrr.io/r/base/library.html)`(`[`ggplot2`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org)`)`\
\
[`ggplot`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggplot.html)`(`\
`  data ``=`` ``bb_sim``,`\
`  `[`aes`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/aes.html)`(`\
`    x ``=`` ``dates``,`\
`    y ``=`` ``intensity`\
`  ``)`\
`)`` ``+`\
`  `[`labs`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html)`(`\
`    y ``=`` ``"Intensity"``,`\
`    x ``=`` ``"Date"`\
`  ``)`` ``+`\
`  `[`geom_line`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_path.html)`(``)`` ``+`\
`  `[`geom_point`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_point.html)`(``)`` ``+`\
`  `[`theme_classic`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/ggtheme.html)`(``)`

![Bacterial blight disease progress over time. Results for wet season
year 2000 at IRRI Zeigler Experiment Station shown. Weather data used to
run the model were obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center POWER
Project funded through the NASA Earth Science Directorate Applied
Science Program.](reference/figures/README-plot-1.png)

Bacterial blight disease progress over time. Results for wet season year
2000 at IRRI Zeigler Experiment Station shown. Weather data used to run
the model were obtained from the NASA Langley Research Center POWER
Project funded through the NASA Earth Science Directorate Applied
Science Program.

## Code of Conduct

Please note that the epicrop project is released with a [Contributor
Code of
Conduct](https://codeberg.org/adamhsparks/epicrop/src/branch/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).
By contributing to this project, you agree to abide by its terms.

## Other Implementations in R

- The EPIRICE model was originally written in R as a part of the
  [{cropsim}](https://github.com/r-forge/cropsim/tree/master/pkg/cropsim)
  package (Hijmans *et al.* 2009).

- The EPIRICE model is also available from CRAN in the
  [{ZeBook}](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ZeBook) package (Brun
  *et al.* 2018) to accompany, “Working with dynamic crop models:
  methods, tools and examples for agriculture and environment” (Wallach
  *et al.* 2018).

(2018). *ZeBook: Working with Dynamic Models for Agriculture and
Environment*. DOI:
[10.32614/CRAN.package.ZeBook](https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.ZeBook)

South Korea. *Agricultural and Forest Meteorology*, 203: 191-207. DOI:
[10.1016/j.agrformet.2015.01.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.agrformet.2015.01.011)

*cropsim*. (2009). Simulation modeling of crops and their diseases. R
package version 0.2-6.

Jorrel Aunario. (2012). Modeling and mapping potential epidemics of rice
diseases globally. *Crop Protection*, Volume 34, Pages 6-17, ISSN
0261-2194 DOI:
[10.1016/j.cropro.2011.11.009](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cropro.2011.11.009).

4:771–90. DOI:
[10.1007/s10658-015-0650-7](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10658-015-0650-7).

[`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
using pre-defined models

  [`sheath_blight()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`tungro()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`modified_kim_leaf_blast()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`modified_kim_sheath_blight()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`leaf_rust()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`s_tritici_blotch()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`bb()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)
  [`bs()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/disease_models.md)

  : Rice and Wheat Disease Models

## Helper Functions for Multiple Simulations

- [`run_epicrop_model()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/run_epicrop_model.md)
  : Run an epicrop disease model across emergence dates and/or locations
- [`build_epicrop_emergence()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/build_epicrop_emergence.md)
  : Build emergence dates from year × month_day combinations
- [`audpc_dt()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/audpc_dt.md)
  : Extract AUDPC Summary as data.table

## SEIR

A susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) model and the main
function that drives {epicrop}

- [`seir()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/seir.md)
  : Susceptible-Exposed-Infectious-Removed (SEIR) Model Framework with
  Lesion Expansion

## Weather Data

Functions for fetching and formatting weather data for use in {epicrop}

- [`get_wth()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/get_wth.md)
  : Get Weather Data for Modelling Disease
- [`fetch_epicrop_weather_list()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/fetch_epicrop_weather_list.md)
  : Fetch weather once (single or multiple locations) and split by
  calendar year
- [`format_wth()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/format_wth.md)
  : Format Weather Data for Use in seir() Simulations

## Miscellaneous

Other functions

- [`get_audpc()`](https://adamhsparks.codeberg.page/epicrop/reference/get_audpc.md)
  : Get AUDPC from epicrop.sim Object
